newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader tries to lure presidential rivals.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader tries to lure presidential rivals.

text.p: Chechen guerrilla leader Aslan Maskhadov, acclaimed winner of Sunday's post-war election in the breakaway region, sought on Thursday to bring his main presidential rival into a future government.

The latest incomplete returns put Maskhadov well ahead of prominent field commander Shamil Basayev, who fuelled fears of a potentially explosive split in rebel ranks with bitter attacks on his former chief-of-staff during the election campaign.

Basayev on Wednesday conceded victory to Maskhadov and said he would not get in his way. He said he planned to quit politics for the computer business but added that if Maskhadov ditched some of his aides he would work for him "even as a janitor".
Mayerbek Vachagayev, spokesman for the quietly-spoken Maskhadov, said that he had not yet made any official offers of posts in his new government but was about to.
"A meeting between Maskhadov and Basayev is now going on and Maskhadov will suggest that Basayev take part in the new power structures," he told Reuters in an interview.
"Basayev will more than likely accept."

Bodyguards at Maskhadov's house in Pervomaiskoye, about five km (three miles) north-west of the regional capital Grozny, said later that Basayev had spent only five minutes with Maskhadov but that the two men had agreed to meet again in two days.
Vachagayev said a meeting between Maskhadov and Chechnya's current leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev was planned for Thursday evening, but did not say what would be on the agenda.
Mumadi Saydayev, chairman of Chechnya's central electoral commission, said the latest returns showed Maskhadov with 63.3 percent of the vote against Basayev's 24.4 percent.
Yandarbiyev was trailing with 10.9 percent, he told Reuters.
Russian news agencies said that both Basayev and Yandarbiyev had complained of violations in the elections, declared free by international observers, but said they accepted the results.
Hardline rebel Salman Raduyev, who led a bloody hostage raid a year ago, said on Wednesday he did not recognise the poll, would not obey Maskhadov and planned terror attacks on Russia.

Both Moscow and Grozny said on Thursday they would not allow Raduyev's inflammatory statements to increase tension in the region. The Chechen authorities promised a tough response to any illegal acts by Raduyev.

Maskhadov's spokesman said that parliament had met on Thursday and proposed three possible dates for the inauguration. They were February 10, the end of the Moslem fast of Ramadan or a week later after runoff parliamentary elections, which are due to be held in 55 out of the 63 voting districts on February 15.
Vachagayev said that Maskhadov wanted one of those dates rather than the third option of a date in two months time.
"But we are not that bothered about that problem because real power already lies with Maskhadov. The ceremony handing over power will be just a formality," Mayarbek told Reuters.
Maskhadov, a former Soviet army colonel, led a ragtag rebel force against the Russian army after Russian President Boris Yeltsin sent troops to Chechnya in December 1994.

Tens of thousands of people died in 21 months of fighting, which ended in a peace deal with Moscow last August. The deal deferred the issue of Chechnya's status for five years in return for the withdrawal of the troops, who had failed to crush the rebels.
Moscow has refused to countenance the idea of an independent Chechnya. But Maskhadov and other Chechens say the region is already independent.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Maskhadov, a former Soviet army colonel, as saying he wanted discussions about Chechnya's status to begin as soon as possible.
